Earvin "Magic" Johnson Jr. was born on August 14, 1959.
Earvin Johnson Sr., Earvin's father, worked as a General Motors assembly worker and a janitor.
Christine, Earvin's mother, worked as a school janitor.
Earvin Johnson Jr. had six siblings and three half-siblings from his father's previous marriage.
Earvin Johnson Jr.'s favorite basketball player growing up was Bill Russell.
Earvin Johnson Jr. idolized players such as Earl Monroe and Marques Haynes.
Earvin Johnson Jr. came from an athletic family; his father played high school basketball in Mississippi, and he learned the finer points of the game from him.
Christine, Earvin's mother, originally from North Carolina, had also played basketball as a child.
By eighth grade, Earvin Johnson Jr. was thinking about a future in basketball.
Earvin Johnson Jr. scored 48 points in a junior high game.
Earvin Johnson Jr.'s plans for high school changed when he learned he would be bused to Everett High School instead of going to Sexton High School.
Everett High School was predominantly white, while Sexton High School was predominantly black.
Racism occurred at Everett High School with rocks being thrown at buses carrying black students and white parents refusing to send their children to school.
Larry Johnson, Earvin's brother, was kicked off the basketball team after a confrontation during practice.
Earvin Johnson Jr. joined the basketball team but became angry when his new teammates ignored him during practice.
Earvin Johnson Jr. nearly got into a fight with another player before head coach George Fox intervened.
Earvin Johnson Jr. accepted his situation and the small group of black students looked to him as their leader.
Earvin Johnson Jr.'s time at Everett High School changed him, teaching him how to understand white people, communicate, and deal with them.

Earvin Johnson Jr. was first dubbed "Magic" by Fred Stabley Jr., a sports writer for the Lansing State Journal, after recording a triple-double of 36 points, 18 rebounds, and 16 assists as a sophomore at Everett High School.
Earvin Johnson Jr.'s mother initially believed that being called "Magic" was sacrilegious due to her strong Christian faith.
Earvin Johnson Jr. led Everett High School to a 27-1 win-loss record in his final high school season while averaging 28.8 points and 16.8 rebounds per game.
Earvin Johnson Jr. dedicated the championship victory to his best friend Reggie Chastine, who was killed in a car accident the previous summer.
Earvin Johnson Jr. finished his high school career with two All-State selections.
Earvin Johnson Jr. was considered at the time to be the best high school player ever to come out of Michigan.
Earvin Johnson Jr. was named to the inaugural McDonald's All-American team, which played in the 1977 Capital Classic.
Earvin Johnson Jr. decided to play close to home and ultimately chose to attend Michigan State University when coach Jud Heathcote told him he could play the point guard position.
Earvin Johnson Jr.'s college decision came down to Michigan and Michigan State in East Lansing.
Earvin Johnson Jr. was initially not aspiring to play professionally, focusing instead on his communication studies major and desire to become a television commentator.
Earvin Johnson Jr. averaged 17.0 points, 7.9 rebounds, and 7.4 assists per game as a freshman at Michigan State University.
Earvin Johnson Jr. led the Spartans to a 25-5 record in his first two years of college basketball.
Earvin Johnson Jr. entered the 1979 NBA draft after two years in college.
Jud Heathcote stepped down as coach of the Spartans after the 1994–95 season, and on June 8, 1995, Earvin Johnson returned to the Breslin Center to play in the Jud Heathcote All-Star Tribute Game.
Earvin Johnson Jr. was drafted first overall by the Los Angeles Lakers in the 1979 NBA draft.
Earvin Johnson Jr. said that what was "most amazing" about joining the Lakers was the chance to play alongside Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, who became the leading scorer in NBA history.
Despite Kareem Abdul-Jabbar's dominance, he had failed to win a championship with the Lakers, and Earvin Johnson was expected to help them achieve that goal.
Lakers coach Jack McKinney had the 6-foot-9-inch (2.06 m) rookie Earvin Johnson play as a point guard, even though incumbent Norm Nixon was already one of the best in the league.
Earvin Johnson Jr. averaged 18.0 points, 7.7 rebounds, and 7.3 assists per game for the season.
Earvin Johnson Jr. was selected to the NBA All-Rookie Team.
Earvin Johnson Jr. was named an NBA All-Star Game starter.
The Lakers compiled a 60-22 record in the regular season and reached the 1980 NBA Finals, where they faced the Philadelphia 76ers.
Earvin Johnson Jr. recorded 42 points, 15 rebounds, 7 assists, and 3 steals in a 123–107 win for the Lakers in Game 6 of the 1980 NBA Finals.
Earvin Johnson Jr. became the only rookie to win the NBA Finals MVP award.
Earvin Johnson Jr.'s clutch performance is still regarded as one of the finest in NBA history.
Earvin Johnson Jr. also became one of four players to win NCAA and NBA championships in consecutive years.
Early in the 1980–81 season, Earvin Johnson suffered torn cartilage in his left knee and missed 45 games.
Earvin Johnson's rehabilitation was the "most down" he had ever felt during that time.

Earvin Johnson returned before the start of the 1981 playoffs but the Lakers' then-assistant and future head coach Pat Riley later said Johnson's much-anticipated return made the Lakers a "divided team".
The 54-win Lakers faced the 40–42 Houston Rockets in the first round of playoffs, where Houston upset the Lakers 2–1 after Earvin Johnson airballed a last-second shot in Game 3.

In 1981, after the 1980–81 season, Earvin Johnson signed a 25-year, $25 million contract with the Lakers (equivalent to $84,000,000 in 2023), which was the highest-paying contract in sports history up to that point.
Early in the 1981–82 season, Earvin Johnson had a heated dispute with Westhead, who Johnson said made the Lakers "slow" and "predictable".
After Earvin Johnson demanded to be traded, Lakers owner Jerry Buss fired Westhead and replaced him with Riley.
Although Earvin Johnson denied responsibility for Westhead's firing, he was booed across the league, even by Laker fans.

Buss was also unhappy with the Lakers' offense and had intended on firing Westhead days before the Westhead–Johnson altercation, but assistant GM Jerry West and GM Bill Sharman had convinced Buss to delay his decision.
Despite off-court troubles, Earvin Johnson averaged 18.6 points, 9.6 rebounds, 9.5 assists, and a league-high 2.7 steals per game in the 1981–82 season.
Earvin Johnson joined Wilt Chamberlain and Oscar Robertson as the only NBA players to tally at least 700 points, 700 rebounds, and 700 assists in the same season.
The Lakers advanced through the 1982 playoffs and faced Philadelphia for the second time in three years in the 1982 NBA Finals.
Earvin Johnson averaged 16.2 points on .533 shooting, 10.8 rebounds, 8.0 assists, and 2.5 steals per game during the championship series against the Sixers.
During the 1982 NBA season, Earvin Johnson had a first of nine consecutive double-double seasons, with 16.8 points, 10.5 assists, and 8.6 rebounds per game.
The Lakers reached the Finals for the third year in a row, where Earvin Johnson's Lakers and Larry Bird's Celtics met for the first time in the postseason.
Earvin Johnson was booed across the league after his return to play with the Lakers.
Earvin Johnson averaged 19.0 points on .403 shooting, 12.5 assists, and 7.8 rebounds per game during a losing effort against Philadelphia in the 1982 NBA Finals.
In the 1984–85 regular season, Earvin Johnson averaged 18.3 points, 12.6 assists, and 6.2 rebounds per game.

The Lakers defeated the Celtics in six games in the 1985 NBA Finals, with Earvin Johnson averaging 18.3 points on .494 shooting, 14.0 assists, and 6.8 rebounds per game during the championship series.
Earvin Johnson again averaged a double-double in the 1985–86 NBA season, with 18.8 points, 12.6 assists, and 5.9 rebounds per game.
The Lakers advanced to the Western Conference Finals but were unable to defeat the Houston Rockets who advanced to the Finals in five games.
In the next season, Earvin Johnson averaged a career-high of 23.9 points, as well as 12.2 assists and 6.3 rebounds per game, earning his first regular season MVP award.
The Lakers met the Celtics for the third time in the NBA Finals, and in Game 4, Earvin Johnson hit a last-second hook shot over Celtics big men Parish and Kevin McHale to win the game 107–106.
Earvin Johnson was awarded his third Finals MVP title after averaging 26.2 points on .541 shooting, 13.0 assists, 8.0 rebounds, and 2.33 steals per game during the 1986 NBA Finals.
Before the 1987–88 NBA season, Lakers coach Pat Riley publicly promised that they would defend the NBA title.
Earvin Johnson had another productive season with averages of 19.6 points, 11.9 assists, and 6.2 rebounds per game despite missing 10 games with a groin injury.

In the 1988 playoffs, the Lakers swept the San Antonio Spurs in 3 games, then survived two 4–3 series against the Utah Jazz and Dallas Mavericks to reach the Finals and face Thomas and the Detroit Pistons.
Earvin Johnson returned to play after a six-game absence due to an ankle sprain and put up a season-high 44 points in 40 minutes during the 1987–88 NBA season.
The game-winning shot, which Earvin Durant dubbed his "junior, junior, junior sky-hook", helped Los Angeles defeat Boston in six games during the 1986 NBA Finals.
Earvin Johnson was one of the most dominant players of his era and known for his extraordinary court vision, passing abilities, and leadership.
Earvin Johnson's career achievements include three NBA Most Valuable Player Awards, three NBA Finals MVPs, nine All-NBA First Team designations, and twelve All-Star games selections.

Earvin Johnson led the league in regular season assists four times and is the NBA's all-time leader in average assists per game in both the regular season (11.19 assists per game) and the playoffs (12.35 assists per game).
Earvin Johnson holds the records for most career playoff assists and most career playoff triple-doubles.
Earvin Johnson was the co-captain of the 1992 United States men's Olympic basketball team ("The Dream Team"), which won the Olympic gold medal in Barcelona.
After leaving the NBA in 1991, Earvin Johnson formed the Magic Johnson All-Stars, a barnstorming team that traveled around the world playing exhibition games.
Earvin Johnson was honored as one of the 50 Greatest Players in NBA History in 1996 and selected to the NBA 75th Anniversary Team in 2021.
Earvin Johnson became a two-time inductee into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame—being enshrined in 2002 for his individual career, and again in 2010 as a member of the "Dream Team".
Earvin Johnson's friendship and rivalry with Boston Celtics star Larry Bird are well documented.
Earvin Johnson has won 14 total championships during his career, one in college, five as an NBA player, and eight as an owner.
